title: Every owner uses ei ole
summary: Negative possession uses the same ei ole with every owner: minulla ei ole, sinulla ei ole, hänellä ei ole, meillä ei ole, teillä ei ole, heillä ei ole.
objectives: Use ei ole to deny possession for any of the six owners.
Recognise the pattern, then produce it with the supporting words shown.

sections.title: How the pattern works
paragraphs: Negative possession uses the same ei ole with every owner: minulla ei ole, sinulla ei ole, hänellä ei ole, meillä ei ole, teillä ei ole, heillä ei ole.
The -lla/-llä phrase identifies the owner. It does not make ei agree with “I”, “we”, or “they”. In these first questions the complete negative noun form is shown.
Hänellä can refer to a man or a woman. Sinulla addresses one person; teillä addresses a group in these tasks. Teillä can also address one person politely when that context is stated.
keyPoints: Use one singular thing and the owner form shown by the prompt.

sections.title: Regular noun forms in these examples
paragraphs: These forms name the thing after ei ole. The prompts show the noun form whenever forming it is outside this lesson’s target.
keyPoints: kissa (“cat”) → kissaa (“a cat”): regular singular partitive
koira (“dog”) → koiraa (“a dog”): regular singular partitive
tyyny (“pillow”) → tyynyä (“a pillow”): regular singular partitive
peli (“game”) → peliä (“a game”): regular singular partitive

examples.english: I do not have a ball.
steps: minulla means “I as the owner”.
For possession, ei supplies “not” and ole is the form of olla after it. Keep ei ole together; minulla does not require en ole.
The complete noun form palloa (“a ball”) is shown here; its formation is taught in the next lesson.

examples.english: You do not have a book.
steps: sinulla means “you as the owner” for one person.
Use sinulla ei ole, not sinulla et ole. The owner phrase does not conjugate the negative verb.
The complete noun form kirjaa (“a book”) is shown here; its formation is taught in the next lesson.

examples.english: She does not have a dog.
steps: hänellä means “he as the owner” or “she as the owner”; this example uses “she”.
Hänellä ei ole can mean “she does not have” or “he does not have”. Both use the same negative frame.
The complete noun form koiraa (“a dog”) is shown here; its formation is taught in the next lesson.

examples.english: We do not have a car.
steps: meillä means “we as the owner”.
With several owners, meillä still takes ei ole, not emme ole.
The complete noun form autoa (“a car”) is shown here; its formation is taught in the next lesson.

examples.english: You do not have a game.
steps: teillä means “you as the owner” for a group.
Teillä still takes ei ole, not ette ole, even though the owner is a group.
The complete noun form peliä (“a game”) is shown here; its formation is taught in the next lesson.

examples.english: They do not have a pen.
steps: heillä means “they as the owner”.
Heillä still takes ei ole, not eivät ole. Only the owner phrase has changed.
The complete noun form kynää (“a pen”) is shown here; its formation is taught in the next lesson.

examples.english: I do not have a cat.
steps: minulla means “I as the owner”.
Changing the thing leaves the fixed ei ole frame unchanged.
The complete noun form kissaa (“a cat”) is shown here; its formation is taught in the next lesson.

examples.english: We do not have a pillow.
steps: meillä means “we as the owner”.
The front vowels in the noun affect its noun ending, not fixed ei ole.
The complete noun form tyynyä (“a pillow”) is shown here; its formation is taught in the next lesson.

commonMistakes: Keep both words ei ole: ei alone leaves the negative possession pattern incomplete.
Use meillä ei ole and heillä ei ole, rather than person-conjugated emme ole or eivät ole.
Use the complete noun form shown in these verb questions; the following lesson teaches how to form it.

pallo + -a = palloa. This is the singular partitive, the noun form used when possession is denied.
